title: Explain a concept to a non-engineer
prompt: Explain eventual consistency to a product manager in at most 150 words. Include exactly one concrete analogy and one practical implication for a feature they might be designing. Avoid jargon such as "replica", "quorum" or "CAP".
system:
You are completing one task from an evaluation suite. Do the task as asked.

Reply with the requested text only, with no preamble about what you are doing.

rubric.name: correct
rubric.description: The explanation is accurate: copies of the data can briefly disagree after a change and then converge. No false claims.

rubric.name: analogy
rubric.description: Contains exactly one concrete analogy, and the analogy actually shows a temporary disagreement that resolves.

rubric.name: implication
rubric.description: Gives one practical product implication a PM could act on (for example a user may briefly see stale data, and when that matters).

rubric.name: plain_language
rubric.description: At most 150 words and free of the banned jargon (replica, quorum, CAP) and of similar unexplained terms.

reference:
Eventual consistency means that after a change is saved, different parts of the system may
briefly disagree about it, and then all catch up.

Think of a chain of shops updating a price. Head office sends the new price, but each shop
changes its shelf labels at a slightly different moment. For a short while, two shops show
different prices. Soon they all match.

The practical implication: right after a user edits something, another screen or another
user may still see the old value for a moment. If you are designing a "like" counter, that
delay is harmless. If you are designing "seats remaining" for ticket sales, it is not, and
the design has to confirm the seat at the moment of purchase instead of trusting the
number on screen.
answers:
Eventual consistency means that after a change is saved, different parts of the system may
briefly disagree about it, and then all catch up.

Think of a chain of shops updating a price. Head office sends the new price, but each shop
changes its shelf labels at a slightly different moment. For a short while, two shops show
different prices. Soon they all match.

The practical implication: right after a user edits something, another screen or another
user may still see the old value for a moment. If you are designing a "like" counter, that
delay is harmless. If you are designing "seats remaining" for ticket sales, it is not, and
the design has to confirm the seat at the moment of purchase instead of trusting the
number on screen.

Eventual consistency is a consistency model used in distributed systems where replicas
converge over time. Under the CAP theorem you can only have two of consistency,
availability and partition tolerance, so many databases choose AP and relax consistency.
Writes are acknowledged before a quorum of replicas has applied them, and anti-entropy
processes such as read repair and gossip reconcile divergent replicas later. It is like a
bank, or like DNS, or like a group chat. This is in contrast to strong consistency, where
linearizability guarantees that every read reflects the latest write.
